summary: This Wikipedia-style article surveys mental health, covering its definitions (including the WHO definition and the tripartite well-being model), history from mental hygiene through deinstitutionalization, global epidemiology and demographic risk groups such as children, the homeless, and refugees, and the causes and social factors that shape it. It also describes the roles of occupational therapy and psychiatric social work, and the stigma and cultural considerations around mental illness. The note is truncated mid-sentence in its poverty section.
one_line: Overview of mental health: definitions, history, global prevalence, demographic risk groups, causes, and the professions that treat mental illness.
key_facts: The WHO defines mental health as a "state of well-being in which the individual realizes his or her abilities, can cope with the normal stresses of life, can work productively and fruitfully, and can contribute to his or her community".
In 2019, about 970 million people worldwide suffered from a mental disorder, with anxiety and depression being the most common.
William Sweetser was the first to coin the term mental hygiene in the mid-19th century.

Dorothea Dix (1802–1887) was an important figure in the development of the "mental hygiene" movement and won federal government support to set up over 30 state psychiatric hospitals from 1840 to 1880.
Emil Kraepelin developed the taxonomy of mental disorders in 1896, which dominated the field for nearly 80 years.
The Community Mental Health Centers Act of 1963 enforced the closure of state-provisioned psychiatric hospitals and restricted admission to patients posing an imminent danger to others or themselves.
The Penrose Hypothesis of 1939 theorized an inverse relationship between prisons' population size and the number of psychiatric hospital beds.
As of 2021, over 22 percent of all Americans over the age of 18 meet the criteria for having a mental illness.
A WHO report estimates the global cost of mental illness at nearly $2.5 trillion in 2010, with a projected increase to over $6 trillion by 2030.
Major depression ranks third among the top 10 leading causes of disease worldwide and is predicted to become the leading cause by 2030.
Suicide is the fourth leading cause of death in 15-19-year-olds.
Of young adults affected by mental illness, 42% went untreated as of 2018.
Among homeless single women and mothers in St. Louis, Missouri, 53% of respondents met diagnostic criteria for PTSD, according to research summarized by Lisa Goodman and colleagues.

In the United States, 60 percent of mental health professionals are clinically trained social workers, 10 percent are psychiatrists, 23 percent are psychologists, and 5 percent are psychiatric nurses.
Unhappily married couples suffer 3–25 times the risk of developing clinical depression.
Clifford Beers founded "Mental Health America – National Committee for Mental Hygiene" and opened the first outpatient mental health clinic in the United States.
